title: The Version of You Everyone Applauds May Be the Version of You God Is Asking You to Stop Performing
paragraphs: The Version of You Everyone Applauds May Be the Version of You God Is Asking You to Stop Performing
What if the most dangerous mask you wear is the one people call “godly”—and what if Jesus loves you too much to let you keep hiding behind it?
There is a version of you that people may love.
The strong version.
The faithful version.
The one who knows what verse to quote when somebody is hurting.
The one who posts Scripture.
The one who says, “God is good,” even when your heart feels like it is collapsing somewhere nobody can see.
The one who serves.
The one who gives.
The one who prays beautifully.
The one people message when their faith is falling apart.
And perhaps the frightening part is this:
Everybody thinks that version of you is doing fine.
Maybe they even admire you.
But God sees the room after everyone leaves.
He sees the phone placed facedown.
The smile disappearing.
The prayer that never gets prayed.
The temptation nobody knows about.
The resentment buried beneath Christian vocabulary.
The secret need to be noticed.
The exhaustion of maintaining an image you are terrified to disappoint.
The private compromises.
The hunger for approval.
The shame.
The loneliness.
The question you would never say at church:
“God… do You still want me when I am not impressive?”
And into that hidden room walks Jesus.
Not the Jesus we sometimes manufacture for public consumption.
Not a mascot for religious success.
Not Someone impressed by polished appearances.
Jesus Christ—the One before whom every mask becomes unnecessary.
And His words in Matthew 6 are uncomfortable precisely because they are spoken to people doing apparently righteous things.
Giving.
Praying.
Seeking God.
These are not obvious acts of rebellion.
That is what makes His warning terrifying.
Jesus says:
“Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them.”
Matthew 6:1
The Greek expression translated “to be seen by them” is πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς—pros to theathēnai autois.
That verb, θεαθῆναι (theathēnai), comes from θεάομαι (theaomai), carrying the idea of being seen, observed, or looked upon.
Jesus puts His finger on something painfully human.
It is possible to do something righteous while secretly craving an audience.
It is possible to speak about God while wanting people to notice us.
It is possible to serve Jesus while becoming addicted to the reputation that serving Jesus gives us.
It is possible to appear spiritually alive while slowly starving inside.
And before we turn this into an accusation against somebody else, perhaps we should sit with the question ourselves.
Who are you when nobody is watching?
Not who does Facebook think you are.
Not who your church thinks you are.
Not who your family thinks you are.
Not who your followers think you are.
Who are you before God?
Because religious reputation can become an idol when protecting the appearance of righteousness becomes more important than living truthfully before the God who sees the hidden person.
Jesus continues:
“Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do…”
Matthew 6:2
The Greek word translated “hypocrites” is ὑποκριταί—hypokritai.

Historically, the related Greek word could refer to an actor or performer. In the New Testament, however, the word carries the moral force of hypocrisy—someone whose outward presentation and inward reality do not agree.
That makes the warning disturbingly personal.
Because spiritual performance does not always look fake.
Sometimes it looks magnificent.
Sometimes people applaud it.
Sometimes people share it.
Sometimes people call it anointing.
Sometimes the performer himself eventually forgets he is performing.
You learn the vocabulary.
You learn when to raise your hands.
You learn what testimony is safe enough to tell.
You learn how much brokenness to reveal without damaging the image.
You learn how to say, “I’m trusting God,” when what you really want to say is:
“I’m exhausted.”
“I’m angry.”
“I’m jealous.”
“I’m struggling with lust.”
“I haven't forgiven them.”
“My prayer life is almost nonexistent.”
“I feel numb when I worship.”
“I keep returning to the same sin.”
“I am terrified people will discover that the person they admire is not the person I see when I am alone.”
So you keep performing.
Because applause is easier than exposure.
Reputation feels safer than repentance.
And being admired can become easier than being known.
But Jesus does something astonishing in this passage.
He repeatedly redirects our attention away from the audience and toward the Father.
When you give secretly, Jesus says:
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”
Matthew 6:4
When you pray, He says:
“Go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret.”
Matthew 6:6
And again:
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”
There is a beautiful phrase underneath those words:
ὁ πατήρ σου ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ
ho patēr sou ho blepōn en tō kryptō
“Your Father who sees in secret.”
Read that again.
Your Father sees.
Not merely your congregation.
Not your followers.
Not the people impressed by you.
Not the people disappointed in you.
Your Father sees.
He sees what nobody applauds.
He sees the prayer whispered through tears.
He sees you closing the browser.
He sees you choosing not to send the message.
He sees the money given quietly.
He sees the apology nobody online will ever know you made.
He sees you opening Scripture when your emotions tell you nothing is happening.
He sees the battle behind the testimony.
He sees the trembling repentance behind the smile.
He sees the Christian who is tired of pretending.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear something Christianity never gives us permission to forget:
God's answer to hypocrisy is not better acting.
It is truth and repentance.
The Gospel does not say, “Become convincing enough that nobody notices your sin.”
The Gospel says that sinners may come into the light because Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally the story of impressive people finally becoming worthy of God.
It is the story of a holy God showing mercy to guilty people through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, your reputation cannot save you.
Your ministry cannot save you.
Your Bible knowledge cannot save you.
Your followers cannot save you.
Your charitable giving cannot save you.
Your Christian vocabulary cannot save you.
Your parents' faith cannot save you.
Your church attendance cannot save you.
Only Christ saves.
Jesus carried sin to the cross, died, and rose again.
The scandal of grace is that the person underneath your carefully managed image is precisely the person Christ commands to repent, believe, and come to Him.
You do not have to clean the mask.
You can put it down.
Maybe that is why this hurts.
Because perhaps you have spent years building a version of yourself that everybody loves.
And now Jesus is asking for the person underneath it.
The frightened person.
The angry person.
The addicted person.
The insecure person.
The person who secretly loves human approval.
The person who has preached truths he has struggled to live.
The woman everyone calls strong who cries where nobody can hear her.
The father who prays over his children but privately wonders why his own heart feels so far from God.
The worship leader singing about surrender while protecting one locked room of the soul.
The pastor feeding everyone while quietly starving.
The young believer terrified that asking honest questions will make everyone think his faith is weak.
The Christian posting about peace while having panic-filled nights.
The person everyone assumes is spiritually successful.
You.
Not your brand.
Not your reputation.
You.
Jesus wants truth in the hidden place.
And this is where grace becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
The One who sees the secret place is also the One who went to the cross.
The God from whom nothing is hidden is the God who made a way for sinners to be forgiven.
So confession is not handing new information to God.
He already knows.
Confession is agreeing with God about what we have been hiding and bringing it into the light.
Repentance is not another performance.
It is surrender.
It says:
“Jesus, I am finished defending what You are asking me to forsake.”
Maybe nobody else knows what that sentence means for you.
God does.
Perhaps it means admitting that your public Christianity has become stronger than your private communion with Christ.
Perhaps it means confessing hidden sin.
Perhaps it means forgiving someone.
Perhaps it means seeking help.
Perhaps it means admitting that you enjoy being thought holy more than you enjoy actually being alone with God.
Perhaps your greatest spiritual danger right now is not that people think too little of you.
Maybe it is that they think so highly of you that you have become afraid to tell the truth.
But what if losing the performance is not losing yourself?
What if it is finally allowing Christ to deal with the real you?
There is freedom in no longer needing to convince everyone that you are okay.
There is freedom in praying when nobody knows.
Giving when nobody applauds.
Repenting without turning repentance into content.
Obeying without announcing it.
Serving without needing recognition.
Opening Scripture without photographing the Bible first.
Worshiping without wondering who noticed.
There is freedom when Jesus becomes enough of an audience.
And there is something profoundly healing about realizing that the Father who sees in secret is not fooled by your best day or surprised by your worst one.
The answer is not to become careless about holiness.
Quite the opposite.
Grace does not make sin insignificant.
Grace makes repentance possible.
The same Christ who forgives calls us to follow Him.
The same Gospel that removes condemnation begins transforming the person who believes.
Grace is not permission to keep the mask.
Grace gives us somewhere safe to put it down.
No performance.
No Christian answer designed to impress anybody.
Just you before God.
What are you exhausted from pretending?
What part of your spiritual reputation have you become afraid to lose?
What would change if you cared more about being known by God than being admired by people?
And what is Jesus asking you to bring into the light?
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “no more hiding.”
Not because typing three words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But perhaps those words can become your public acknowledgment that you are finished pretending everything is fine.
If your spirit is exhausted and you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ has already begun dismantling an old version of you and rebuilding your life through grace, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And read the other comments.
Pray for someone.
Encourage someone.
Remind someone that repentance is not the end of their story.
Maybe somebody needs your testimony more than they need another polished Christian performance.
Not to expose them.
To remind them they do not have to carry the mask alone.
Not as proof that you are spiritual.
That would miss everything Jesus just taught us.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ—not through purchasing access to a page.
There may come a night when applause feels empty and the mask becomes unbearably heavy.
Come back and remember Matthew 6.
Your Father sees in secret.
Because somewhere tonight there may be a Christian surrounded by people who admire a version of them they can barely keep alive.
They do not need another lesson in pretending.
They need Jesus.
They need repentance.
They need grace.
They need to discover that being exposed before the mercy of Christ can be infinitely better than being applauded behind a mask.
The world may applaud the performance.
Jesus came for the person underneath it.
And perhaps the greatest scandal is this:
When the mask finally falls, grace does not run away.
Christ calls you into the light.
And when Jesus gets hold of the truth you were terrified to reveal, the collapse of your performance may become the beginning of your freedom.
You spent years protecting the version of you everyone applauded—while Jesus was waiting in the secret place for the person underneath.
